questions.question_text:
In appreciation of the social improvements completed in a town, a wealthy philanthropist
decided to gift Rs 750 to each male senior citizen in the town and Rs 1000 to each female
senior citizen. Altogether, there were 300 senior citizens eligible for this gift. However,
only 8/9th of the eligible men and 2/3rd of the eligible women claimed the gift. How much
money (in Rupees) did the philanthropist give away in total?
questions.subtopic: Numerical computation and estimation: ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms, permutations and combinations, series
questions.explaination: Let $M$ and $W$ be eligible men and women, with $M + W = 300$. Number claiming pension is $\frac{8}{9}M$ men and $\frac{2}{3}W$ women. Total pension claimed $= \frac{8}{9}M(750) + \frac{2}{3}W(1000) = \frac{2000}{3}M + \frac{2000}{3}W = \frac{2000}{3}(M + W) = \frac{2000}{3}(300) = 2{,}00{,}000$.

questions.question_text:
In a party, 60% of the invited guests are male and 40% are female. If 80% of the invited
guests attended the party and if all the invited female guests attended, what would be the
ratio of males to females among the attendees in the party?
questions.subtopic: Numerical computation and estimation: ratios, percentages, powers, exponents and logarithms, permutations and combinations, series
questions.explaination: Out of 100 invited guests, 60 are male and 40 are female. Since 80 guests attend and all 40 invited females attend, the remaining $80 - 40 = 40$ attendees must be male. Thus, the ratio of attending males to attending females is $40 : 40 = 1 : 1$.

questions.question_text:
A six sided unbiased die with four green faces and two red faces is rolled seven times.
Which of the following combinations is the most likely outcome of the experiment?

options.A: Three green faces and four red faces.
options.B: Four green faces and three red faces.
options.C: Five green faces and two red faces.
options.D: Six green faces and one red face.

questions.explaination: The number of green faces $X$ follows a Binomial distribution $B(n=7, p=4/6=2/3)$. The mode of a binomial distribution is $\lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor = \lfloor 8 \times \frac{2}{3} \rfloor = \lfloor 5.33 \rfloor = 5$. Thus, the most likely outcome is 5 green faces and $7 - 5 = 2$ red faces.
questions.question_text_latex: A six sided unbiased die with four green faces and two red faces is rolled seven times. Which of the following combinations is the most likely outcome of the experiment?

options_latex.A: Three green faces and four red faces
options_latex.B: Four green faces and three red faces
options_latex.C: Five green faces and two red faces
options_latex.D: Six green faces and one red face

questions.question_text:
Let N be the set of natural numbers. Consider the following sets.
P: Set of Rational numbers (positive and negative)
Q: Set of functions from {0, 1} to N
R: Set of functions from N to {0, 1}
S: Set of finite subsets of N.

Which of the sets above are countable?
questions.subtopic: Sets, relations, functions, partial orders and lattices
questions.explaination: Set $P$ (rationals) is countably infinite. Set $Q$ (functions $\{0, 1\} \to \mathbb{N}$) is equivalent to $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, which is countable. Set $S$ (finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$) is countable. Set $R$ (functions $\mathbb{N} \to \{0, 1\}$) is equivalent to the power set $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ and has cardinality $2^{\aleph_0}$, which is uncountable. Hence, $P$, $Q$, and $S$ are countable.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
    \item[$P$:] The set of all rational numbers between 0 and 1.
    \item[$Q$:] The set of all functions from $\{0, 1\}$ to $\mathbb{N}$.
    \item[$R$:] The set of all functions from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\{0, 1\}$.
    \item[$S$:] The set of all finite subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
\end{itemize}
Which of the sets above are countable?

questions.question_text:
Let G be a simple undirected graph. Let TD be a depth first search tree of G. Let TB be a
breadth first search tree of G. Consider the following statements.
(I) No edge of G is a cross edge with respect to TD. (A cross edge in G is between two
nodes neither of which is an ancestor of the other in TD.)
(II) For every edge (u,v) of G, if u is at depth i and v is at depth j in TB, then |𝑖−𝑗| = 1.
Which of the statements above must necessarily be true?
questions.subtopic: Graph traversals, minimum spanning trees, shortest paths
questions.explaination: In a DFS tree of an undirected graph, every non-tree edge is a back edge connecting an ancestor and a descendant, so forward and cross edges do not exist; thus statement I is necessarily true. In a BFS tree, cross edges can connect vertices at the same level ($|i - j| = 0$), so statement II is false.

    \item For every edge $(u, v)$ of $G$, if $u$ is at depth $i$ and $v$ is at depth $j$ in $T_B$, then $|i - j| = 1$.
\end{enumerate}
Which of the statements above is/are necessarily TRUE?

Consider the unsigned 8-bit fixed point binary number representation below,
b7 b6 b5 b4 b3 . b2 b1 b0
where the position of the binary point is between b3 and b2. Assume b7 is the most significant
bit. Some of the decimal numbers listed below cannot be represented exactly in the above
representation:
(i)
31.500 (ii) 0.875 (iii) 12.100 (iv) 3.001

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.A: None of (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) can be exactly represented
options.C: Only (iii) and (iv) cannot be exactly represented
options.D: Only (i) and (ii) cannot be exactly represented

questions.subtopic: Number representations and computer arithmetic (fixed and floating point)
questions.explaination: The fractional portion uses 3 bits ($b_2 b_1 b_0$), so the fractional precision is $2^{-3} = 0.125$. Any representable fraction must be an integer multiple of $0.125$: $0.500 = 4 \times 0.125$ (i) and $0.875 = 7 \times 0.125$ (ii) are exact multiples, while $0.100$ and $0.001$ are not.

Consider the following problems. 𝐿(𝐺) denotes the language generated by a grammar 𝐺.
𝐿(𝑀) denotes the language accepted by a machine 𝑀.
(I)
For an unrestricted grammar 𝐺 and a string 𝑤, whether 𝑤∈𝐿(𝐺)
(II)
Given a Turing machine M, whether L(M) is regular
(III)
Given two grammars 𝐺1 and 𝐺2, whether 𝐿(𝐺1) = 𝐿(𝐺2)
(IV)
Given an NFA N, whether there is a deterministic PDA P such that N and P
accept the same language.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

options.A: Only I and II are undecidable
options.C: Only II and IV are undecidable
options.D: Only I, II and III are undecidable

questions.explaination: Problem I (membership for unrestricted grammars) is undecidable. Problem II (testing if a TM accepts a regular language) is undecidable by Rice's theorem. Problem III (equivalence of CFGs) is undecidable. Problem IV asks whether a regular language (NFA) equals a deterministic context-free language (DPDA), which is decidable. Hence, I, II, and III are undecidable.

the alphabet {a,b,c}.

𝑇1: 𝑎? (𝑏|𝑐)∗𝑎

sequence of tokens it outputs?
questions.explaination: A lexical analyzer applies the longest match rule. For input `bbaacabc`, pattern $T_3 = c?(b|a)^*c$ matches prefix `bbaac` (starts without $c$, matches $(b|a)^* = bbaa$, ends with $c$), consuming `bbaac` as token $T_3$. The remaining string is `abc`, which also matches $T_3$ (starts without $c$, $(b|a)^* = ab$, ends with $c$). Hence the recognized sequence of tokens is $T_3 T_3$.

Consider the relations r(A, B) and s(B, C), where s.B is a primary key and r.B is a foreign
key referencing s.B. Consider the query

Q: 𝑟⋈(𝜎𝐵<5(𝑠))

Let LOJ denote the natural left outer-join operation. Assume that r and s contain no null
values.

Which one of the following queries is NOT equivalent to Q?
questions.subtopic: Relational model: relational algebra, tuple calculus, SQL
questions.explaination: Query $Q$ inner joins $r$ with $\sigma_{B < 5}(s)$, which discards all tuples from $r$ where $B \ge 5$. Option (C) performs a left outer join between $r$ and $\sigma_{B < 5}(s)$, which retains all tuples from $r$ (filling missing $C$ values with NULL for $B \ge 5$), so its result is NOT equivalent to $Q$.

questions.question_text:
Consider the following four relational schemas. For each schema, all non-trivial functional
dependencies are listed. The underlined attributes are the respective primary keys.

Schema I: Registration (rollno, courses)
Field ‘courses’ is a set-valued attribute containing the set of courses a student has
registered for.
Non-trivial functional dependency:
rollno → courses

Schema II: Registration (rollno, courseid, email)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid → email
email → rollno

Schema III: Registration (rollno, courseid, marks, grade)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid → marks, grade
marks → grade

Schema IV: Registration (rollno, courseid, credit)
Non-trivial functional dependencies:
rollno, courseid → credit
courseid → credit

Which one of the relational schemas above is in 3NF but not in BCNF?
questions.explaination: In Schema II, the functional dependencies are $rollno \to email$ and $email \to rollno$. The candidate keys are $\{rollno, courseid\}$ and $\{email, courseid\}$. In $email \to rollno$, the left side is not a superkey (violating BCNF), but the right side $rollno$ is a prime attribute (satisfying 3NF). Hence Schema II is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

questions.question_text:
Let G be a graph with 100! vertices, with each vertex labelled by a distinct permutation of
the numbers 1,2, … , 100. There is an edge between vertices 𝑢 and 𝑣 if and only if the label
of 𝑢 can be obtained by swapping two adjacent numbers in the label of 𝑣. Let 𝑦 denote the
degree of a vertex in G, and 𝑧 denote the number of connected components in G.
Then, 𝑦 + 10𝑧 = _____.
questions.explaination: Each permutation of length 100 has 99 pairs of adjacent elements that can be swapped, so the degree of each vertex is $y = 99$. Adjacent transpositions generate the entire symmetric group $S_{100}$, meaning every permutation is reachable from any other; thus the graph is connected, giving $z = 1$ connected component. Hence $y + 10z = 99 + 10(1) = 109$.
questions.question_text_latex: Let $G$ be a graph with $100!$ vertices, with each vertex labelled by a distinct permutation of the numbers $1, 2, \dots, 100$. There is an edge between two vertices if and only if the permutation of one can be obtained by swapping two adjacent elements of the other. Let $y$ be the degree of a vertex in $G$ and $z$ be the number of connected components in $G$. Then $y + 10z =$ \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Consider Guwahati (G) and Delhi (D) whose temperatures can be classified as high (𝐻),
medium (𝑀) and low (𝐿). Let 𝑃(𝐻𝐺) denote the probability that Guwahati has high
temperature. Similarly, 𝑃(𝑀𝐺) and 𝑃(𝐿𝐺) denotes the probability of Guwahati having
medium and low temperatures respectively. Similarly, we use 𝑃(𝐻𝐷), 𝑃(𝑀𝐷) and 𝑃(𝐿𝐷) for
Delhi.

The following table gives the conditional probabilities for Delhi’s temperature given
Guwahati’s temperature.
𝐻𝐷
𝑀𝐷
𝐿𝐷
𝐻𝐺
0.40
0.48
0.12
𝑀𝐺
0.10
0.65
0.25
𝐿𝐺
0.01
0.50
0.49

Consider the first row in the table above. The first entry denotes that if Guwahati has high
temperature (𝐻𝐺) then the probability of Delhi also having a high temperature (𝐻𝐷) is 0.40;
i.e., 𝑃(𝐻𝐷|𝐻𝐺) = 0.40. Similarly, the next two entries are 𝑃(𝑀𝐷|𝐻𝐺) = 0.48 and
𝑃(𝐿𝐷|𝐻𝐺) = 0.12. Similarly for the other rows.

If it is known that 𝑃(𝐻𝐺) = 0.2, 𝑃(𝑀𝐺) = 0.5, and 𝑃(𝐿𝐺) = 0.3, then the probability
(correct to two decimal places) that Guwahati has high temperature given that Delhi has high
temperature is _______.
questions.explaination: Using the law of total probability, the probability of high temperature in Delhi is $P(H_D) = 0.2(0.40) + 0.5(0.10) + 0.3(0.01) = 0.08 + 0.05 + 0.003 = 0.133$. By Bayes' theorem, $P(H_G \mid H_D) = \frac{P(H_G \cap H_D)}{P(H_D)} = \frac{0.08}{0.133} \approx 0.6015$, which falls in the range $0.60$ to $0.62$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider Guwahati ($G$) and Delhi ($D$) whose temperatures can be classified as high ($H$), medium ($M$) and low ($L$). Let $P(H_G) = 0.2$, $P(M_G) = 0.5$, and $P(L_G) = 0.3$ be the probabilities that Guwahati has high, medium, and low temperatures, respectively. Given $P(H_D \mid H_G) = 0.40$, $P(H_D \mid M_G) = 0.10$, and $P(H_D \mid L_G) = 0.01$, the conditional probability $P(H_G \mid H_D)$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_. (Answer correct to two decimal places)

questions.explaination: In `Count(x, y)`, outer recursion on $y$ runs for $y = 1024, 1023, \dots, 2$ ($1023$ values). For each $y$, the inner branch halves $x$ until $x = 1$: starting from $x = 1024$, this loop prints 10 times (since $\log_2(1024) = 10$). Total prints $= 1023 \times 10 = 10230$.

questions.question_text:
The number of possible min-heaps containing each value from {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}exactly once
is _____.
questions.subtopic: Trees, binary search trees, binary heaps
questions.explaination: In a min-heap of 7 elements, the root must contain the minimum element (1). The left subtree has size 3 and the right subtree has size 3. Choosing 3 elements for the left subtree from the remaining 6 elements can be done in $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ ways. A 3-element min-heap has $\binom{2}{1} = 2$ valid configurations. Hence, total valid min-heaps $= 20 \times 2 \times 2 = 80$.
questions.question_text_latex: The number of possible min-heaps containing each value from $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$ exactly once is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Consider the weights and values of items listed below. Note that there is only one unit of
each item.
Item number
Weight
(in Kgs)
Value
(in Rupees)
1
10
60
2
7
28
3
4
20
4
2
24

The task is to pick a subset of these items such that their total weight is no more than 11 Kgs
and their total value is maximized. Moreover, no item may be split. The total value of items
picked by an optimal algorithm is denoted by 𝑉opt. A greedy algorithm sorts the items by
their value-to-weight ratios in descending order and packs them greedily, starting from the
first item in the ordered list. The total value of items picked by the greedy algorithm is
denoted by 𝑉greedy.

The value of 𝑉opt −𝑉greedy is ____________.
questions.subtopic: Algorithm design techniques: greedy, dynamic programming and divide-and-conquer
questions.explaination: Value-to-weight ratios: Item 4 ($24/2 = 12$), Item 1 ($60/10 = 6$), Item 3 ($20/4 = 5$), Item 2 ($28/7 = 4$). The heuristic sorts by ratio and greedily takes Item 4 (wt 2, remaining 9); Item 1 does not fit ($10 > 9$); Item 3 fits (wt 4, remaining 5); Item 2 does not fit ($7 > 5$), yielding $V_{\text{heuristic}} = 24 + 20 = 44$. The optimal 0/1 knapsack selection picks Item 1 (wt 10, val 60). Thus $V_{\text{opt}} - V_{\text{heuristic}} = 60 - 44 = 16$.

questions.question_text:
The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has the following stages: Instruction Fetch (IF),
Instruction Decode (ID), Operand Fetch (OF), Perform Operation (PO) and Writeback (WB).
The IF, ID, OF and WB stages take 1 clock cycle each for every instruction. Consider a
sequence of 100 instructions. In the PO stage, 40 instructions take 3 clock cycles each, 35
instructions take 2 clock cycles each, and the remaining 25 instructions take 1 clock cycle
each. Assume that there are no data hazards and no control hazards.

The number of clock cycles required for completion of execution of the sequence of
instructions is ______.
questions.explaination: For 100 instructions in a 5-stage pipeline without branch delays, ideal cycles $= 5 + (100 - 1) = 104$. The PO stage causes pipeline stalls when operand evaluation takes extra cycles: 40 instructions require 3 cycles (2 extra cycles $\implies 40 \times 2 = 80$ stall cycles) and 35 instructions require 2 cycles (1 extra cycle $\implies 35 \times 1 = 35$ stall cycles). Total clock cycles $= 104 + 80 + 35 = 219$.
questions.question_text_latex: The instruction pipeline of a RISC processor has five stages: Instruction Fetch (IF), Instruction Decode (ID), Perform Operation (PO), Operand Read (OR), and Write Back (WB). Each stage takes 1 clock cycle except PO. For a sequence of 100 instructions, 40 instructions require 3 clock cycles in PO, 35 instructions require 2 clock cycles in PO, and the remaining 25 instructions require 1 clock cycle in PO. Assuming no memory stalls or branch delays, the total number of clock cycles to execute the 100 instructions is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
A processor has 16 integer registers (R0, R1, .. , R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0,
F1,… , F63). It uses a 2-byte instruction format. There are four categories of instructions:
Type-1, Type-2, Type-3, and Type-4. Type-1 category consists of four instructions, each
with 3 integer register operands (3Rs). Type-2 category consists of eight instructions, each
with 2 floating point register operands (2Fs). Type-3 category consists of fourteen
instructions, each with one integer register operand and one floating point register operand
(1R+1F). Type-4 category consists of N instructions, each with a floating point register
operand (1F).

The maximum value of N is __________.
questions.explaination: A 16-bit instruction space has $2^{16} = 65536$ encodings. Type-1: 4 instructions with $3 \times 4\text{-bit}$ registers consume $4 \times 2^{12} = 16384$. Type-2: 8 instructions with $2 \times 6\text{-bit}$ registers consume $8 \times 2^{12} = 32768$. Type-3: 14 instructions with 4-bit and 6-bit registers consume $14 \times 2^{10} = 14336$. Remaining encodings $= 65536 - (16384 + 32768 + 14336) = 2048$. Each Type-4 instruction uses one 6-bit register ($2^6 = 64$ encodings). Thus, maximum $N = 2048 / 64 = 32$.
questions.question_text_latex:
A processor has 16 integer registers (R0 to R15) and 64 floating point registers (F0 to F63). It uses a 16-bit instruction format. Four types of instructions are supported:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, nosep]
    \item Type-1: Opcode with three integer register operands
    \item Type-2: Opcode with two floating point register operands
    \item Type-3: Opcode with one integer and one floating point register operand
    \item Type-4: Opcode with one floating point register operand
\end{itemize}
If there are 4 Type-1, 8 Type-2, and 14 Type-3 instructions, the maximum number of Type-4 instructions that can be supported is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Given a language 𝐿, define 𝐿𝑖 as follows:
𝐿0 = {𝜀}
𝐿𝑖= 𝐿𝑖−1 ⋅𝐿 𝑓𝑜𝑟 𝑎𝑙𝑙 𝑖> 0

The order of a language L is defined as the smallest k such that 𝐿𝑘= 𝐿𝑘+1.
Consider the language L1 (over alphabet 0) accepted by the following automaton.

The order of L1 is _____.
0
0
0
questions.explaination: The given automaton on alphabet $\{0\}$ accepts $L = \{0, 00, 000, \dots\} = 0^+$. Its powers are $L^2 = \{0^k \mid k \ge 2\}$, $L^3 = \{0^k \mid k \ge 3\}$. For the language of strings accepted by the automaton, the smallest integer $k$ satisfying $L^k = L^{k+1}$ is 2.
questions.question_text_latex: Given a language $L$, define $L^i$ as $L^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$ and $L^i = L^{i-1} \cdot L$ for $i > 0$. The order of a language $L$ is defined as the smallest $k$ such that $L^k = L^{k+1}$. Consider the finite automaton accepting $L$ over $\{0\}$ where states accept strings of positive length. The order of language $L$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Consider a storage disk with 4 platters (numbered as 0, 1, 2 and 3), 200 cylinders (numbered
as 0, 1, … , 199), and 256 sectors per track (numbered as 0, 1, … , 255). The following 6
disk requests of the form [sector number, cylinder number, platter number] are received by
the disk controller at the same time:
[120, 72, 2] , [180, 134, 1] , [60, 20, 0] , [212, 86, 3] , [56, 116, 2] , [118, 16, 1]

Currently the head is positioned at sector number 100 of cylinder 80, and is moving towards
higher cylinder numbers. The average power dissipation in moving the head over 100
cylinders is 20 milliwatts and for reversing the direction of the head movement once is 15
milliwatts. Power dissipation associated with rotational latency and switching of head
between different platters is negligible.

The total power consumption in milliwatts to satisfy all of the above disk requests using the
Shortest Seek Time First disk scheduling algorithm is _______.
questions.explaination: Using Shortest Seek Time First (SSTF) starting at cylinder 80: closest is 86 (diff 6, upward), then 72 (diff 14, downward $\implies$ reversal 1), then 116 (diff 44, upward $\implies$ reversal 2), then 134 (diff 18, upward), then 20 (diff 114, downward $\implies$ reversal 3), and finally 16 (diff 4, downward). Total cylinder distance $= 6 + 14 + 44 + 18 + 114 + 4 = 200$. Head movement power $= 200 \times 0.2\text{ mW} = 40\text{ mW}$. Direction reversals $= 3 \times 15\text{ mW} = 45\text{ mW}$. Total power consumed $= 40 + 45 = 85\text{ mW}$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider a storage disk with 200 cylinders (0 to 199). Requests arrive for cylinders: 16, 20, 72, 86, 116, 134. The read/write head is currently at cylinder 80 and moving towards higher cylinder numbers. The SSTF algorithm is used. The disk arm consumes 0.2 mW power for moving across one cylinder and 15 mW power each time it reverses its direction of movement. The total power consumed (in mW) to service all requests is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

questions.question_text:
Consider an IP packet with a length of 4,500 bytes that includes a 20-byte IPv4 header and
a 40-byte TCP header. The packet is forwarded to an IPv4 router that supports a Maximum
Transmission Unit (MTU) of 600 bytes. Assume that the length of the IP header in all the
outgoing fragments of this packet is 20 bytes. Assume that the fragmentation offset value
stored in the first fragment is 0.

The fragmentation offset value stored in the third fragment is _______.
questions.subtopic: Fragmentation and IP addressing, IPv4, CIDR notation
questions.explaination: Total payload to fragment $= 4500 - 20 = 4480$ bytes. With $\text{MTU} = 600$, maximum payload per fragment must be a multiple of 8: $\lfloor (600 - 20) / 8 \rfloor \times 8 = 72 \times 8 = 576$ bytes. Fragment 1 carries bytes 0 to 575 (offset 0). Fragment 2 carries bytes 576 to 1151 (offset $576/8 = 72$). Fragment 3 carries bytes 1152 onwards, so its fragment offset field is $\frac{1152}{8} = 144$.
questions.question_text_latex: Consider an IP packet with a length of 4,500 bytes that includes a 20-byte IPv4 header and a 40-byte TCP header. The packet is forwarded across an IP network with an MTU of 600 bytes. The value of the fragment offset field in the third fragment (in 8-byte units) is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.
